<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\emph{(\textbf{\cite{Naka-Taka}})}. The curves $\gamma$ and $\bar{\gamma}$ are \textbf{ Bertrand mates} if there exists a smooth function $\lambda :I \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $\bar{\gamma}(t)=\gamma(t)+\lambda(t)N(t)$ and $N(t)=\pm\bar{N}(t)$, for all $t \in I$. Moreover, we say that $\gamma : I \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 $ is a \textbf{Bertrand curve} if there exists another non-degenerate curve $\bar{\gamma} : I \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 $ such that $\gamma$ and $\bar{\gamma}$ 
		are Bertrand mates.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\emph{(\textbf{\cite[p.~96]{Lip}})}. A curve $\gamma : I \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$ is a \textbf{Bertrand curve} if and only if there exist nonzero real numbers $A, B$ such that
		\[
		A\kappa(s)+B\tau(s)=1, \; \forall \; s \in [0,L].
		\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\emph{(\textbf{\cite{Izu-Take}})}.
		The vector $D(s)=\tau(s)T(s)+\kappa(s)B(s)$, associated with an unit speed curve $\gamma:[0,L] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$,  is called the \textbf{Darboux vector field} of $\gamma$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\emph{(\textbf{\cite{Izu-Take}})}. The vector field $$
		\tilde{D}(s)=\dfrac{\tau}{\kappa}(s)T(s)+B(s)
		$$
		along $\gamma$, under the condition that $\kappa(s) \neq 0$, $ \forall \; s \in [0,L]$, is called the \textbf{modified Darboux vector field} of $\gamma$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\emph{(\textbf{\cite{Izu-Take}})}. A map $F_{(\gamma, \delta)}:I \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$, defined by 
		$$F_{(\gamma, \delta)}(t,u)=\gamma(t)+u\delta(t),$$
		where $\gamma : I \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$, $\delta : I \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^*$ are smooth mappings and $I$ is an open interval, is called a \textbf{ruled surface} in $\mathbb{R}^3$. The curve $\gamma$ is called the \textbf{base curve} and $\delta$ is called the \textbf{director curve}. Note that the straightlines $u \mapsto \gamma(t)+u\delta(t)$ are called \textbf{rulings}.
		We also remind that a ruled surface associated to a spatial curve $\gamma$ with $\kappa(s)\neq0$, $\forall \; s \in [0,L]$, which is defined by 
		$$F_{(\gamma,\tilde{D})}(s,u)=\gamma(s)+u\tilde{D}(s),$$
		is called the \textbf{rectifying developable} of $\gamma$. Particularly, the ruled surface 
		\begin{equation} \label{Prin-Norm-Surf}
			F_{(\gamma,N)}(s,u)=\gamma(s)+uN(s),
		\end{equation}
		is called the \textbf{principal normal surface} of $\gamma$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def R-C}
		\emph{(\textbf{\cite{Chen}})}.  A unit curve $\gamma: [0,L] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$, defined by
		\begin{equation} \label{Rec-Curve}
			\gamma(s)=\lambda(s)T(s)+\mu(s)B(s),
		\end{equation}
		where $\lambda(s), \; \mu(s)$ are some functions, is called a \textbf{rectifying curve} in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{Th R-C}
		\emph{(\textbf{\cite{Kim-Chu-Cho}})}. The unit speed curve $\gamma : [0,L] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$ is a rectifying curve if and only if there exist the constants $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{R}, \; a_1 \neq 0$, such that
		\begin{equation} \label{R-C cond}
			\dfrac{\tau(s)}{\kappa(s)} = a_1s+a_2,\;\forall \; s\in [0,L].
		\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
By Definition $\ref{def R-C}$, Theorem \ref{Th R-C} and Fr\'{e}net-Serret formulas (\ref{F-S}), we remark that a rectifying curve can be written as:
		\begin{equation} \label{New R-C}
			\gamma(s)=\left ( s + \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} \right )T(s)+\dfrac{1}{a_1}B(s),
		\end{equation}
		for any $s \in [0,L]$ and $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{R}, \; a_1 \neq 0$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
The curvatures of the ruled normal surface associated with the rectifying curve (\ref{New R-C}), which is parametrized by (\ref{R-N-S}), are:
		\begin{itemize}
			\item [1.] The \textbf{Gaussian curvature} $K(s,u)$ is given by
			\begin{equation} \label{G-C}
				K(s,u)=-\dfrac{\tau^2(s)}{\left [ (1-u\kappa(s))^2 + (u\tau(s))^2 \right ]^2}, \quad \forall \; s \in [0,L], u \in \mathbb{R};
			\end{equation}
			
			\item [2.] The \textbf{mean curvature} $H(s,u)$ is given by
			\begin{equation} \label{M-C}
				H(s,u)=\dfrac{u\left [ \tau'(s)+u(\kappa'(s)\tau(s)-\kappa(s)\tau'(s)) \right ]}{2\left [ (1-u\kappa(s))^2+(u\tau(s))^2 \right ]^{3/2}}, \quad \forall \; s \in [0,L], u \in \mathbb{R}. 
			\end{equation}
		\end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We remind the formulas for Gaussian curvature and mean curvature:
		\begin{equation*}
			K=\frac{ln-m^2}{EG-F^2}, \quad
			H=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{lG-2mF+nE}{EG-F^2},
		\end{equation*}
		where $E, \; F, \; G$ are the coefficients of the first fundamental form and $l, \; m, \; n$ are the coefficients of the second fundamental form. 
		
		By direct computation, we obtain
		\[
		E=(1-u\kappa(s))^2+(u\tau(s))^2, \; F=0, \; G=1,
		\]
		\[
		l=\dfrac{u[\tau'(s)+u(\kappa'(s)\tau(s)-\kappa(s)\tau'(s))]}{\sqrt{E}}, \; m=\dfrac{\tau(s)}{\sqrt{E}}, \; n=0,
		\]
		where $ s \in [0,L], u \in \mathbb{R}$.
		Replacing into the curvature formulas mentioned above, we obtain what we were looking for.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
All points of the ruled normal surface associated with a rectifying curve are hyperbolic ones.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Because we have for any rectifying curve $\tau(s)\neq 0, \;\forall \; s \in [0,L] $, from formula (\ref{G-C}) it follows that the inequality $K(s,u)<0$, $\forall \; u\in \mathbb{R}$, $s \in [0,L]$, holds good.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{Not minimal}
		The ruled normal surface associated with a rectifying curve is never minimal one.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We suppose that the ruled normal surface associated with a rectifying curve is minimal, that is $H\equiv0$.
		From (\ref{M-C}), it follows that we obtain for all $s \in [0,L]$:
		$$\left\{ \begin{array}{l}
			\tau'(s)=0 \\
			\kappa'(s)\tau(s)-\kappa(s)\tau'(s)=0
		\end{array} \right. \Leftrightarrow
		\left\{ \begin{array}{l}
			\tau(s)=C_1, \; C_1\in \mathbb{R} \medskip\\
			\dfrac{\kappa'(s)}{\kappa(s)}=\dfrac{\tau'(s)}{\tau(s)}
		\end{array} \right. \Leftrightarrow	$$
		$$
		\Leftrightarrow \left\{ \begin{array}{l}
			\tau(s)=C_1, \; C_1 \in \mathbb{R} \medskip\\
			\kappa(s)=C_2\tau(s), \; C_2 >0.
		\end{array} \right.
		$$
		
		In conclusion, we infer that we have 
		$$\dfrac{\tau(s)}{\kappa(s)}= \mbox{constant},$$ which contradicts the hypothesis that the curve is rectifying.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
The curve $\gamma : [0,L] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3, \; \gamma(s)=(x(s),y(s),z(s))$, defined by
		\begin{equation} \label{Ex 1}
			\begin{array}{l}
				x(s) =   \pm \dfrac{b_1}{a_1} \ln \left |(a_1s+a_2)+\sqrt{1+(a_1s+a_2)^2} \right | + C_3,  \medskip\\
				y(s) =  \pm \dfrac{b_2}{a_1} \ln \left |(a_1s+a_2)+\sqrt{1+(a_1s+a_2)^2} \right | + C_4,   \medskip\\
				z(s) =   \pm \dfrac{\sqrt{1+(a_1s+a_2)^2}}{a_1} + C_5, \\
			\end{array}
		\end{equation} 
		where $b_1, b_2 \in [-1,1], \; b_1^2+b_2^2=1$, $a_1, a_2, C_3, C_4, C_5 \in \mathbb{R}$ and $a_1 \neq 0$, has the following torsion and curvature:
		\begin{equation} \label{C-T}
			\tau(s) = \pm \dfrac{2a_1(a_1s+a_2)}{1+(a_1s+a_2)^2}, \quad \kappa(s) = \pm \dfrac{a_1}{1+(a_1s+a_2)^2}.
		\end{equation}
		In other words, we have $\tau(s)/\kappa(s)=2(a_1s+a_2)$, that is $\gamma(s)$ is a rectifying curve.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{Rec not Bert}
		No curve can be simultaneously a rectifying curve and a Bertrand curve.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
From paper \cite{Izu-Take}, we know that the normal ruled surfaces attached to Bertrand curves are always minimal. According to Proposition \ref{Not minimal}, the normal ruled surfaces attached to rectifying curves cannot be minimal. We get a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
There are no curves having "a priori" the curvature and torsion given by
		\[
		\kappa(s)=\dfrac{1}{A+B(a_1s+a_2)}, \; \tau(s)=\dfrac{a_1s+a_2}{A+B(a_1s+a_2)},
		\]
		where $\forall \; s \in [0,L], A, B, a_1 \in \mathbb{R}^*$ and $a_2 \in \mathbb{R}$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
A curve $\gamma(s)$ with above curvature and torsion are, at the same time, rectifying and Bertrand. According with Theorem \ref{Rec not Bert}, we conclude that there is no curve whose curvature and torsion can be expressed as shown above.  \medskip
<!-- end proof-5 -->
